section_label: CHAPTER TITLE: TEN PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS
text: REFERENCE BOOK: PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS, N. GREGORY MANKIW, CENGAGE LEARNING, 7TH ED. OBJECTIVE • By the end of this chapter, the pupil will be able- • To understand the foundational principles guiding economic thinking. • To explain how individuals face trade-offs in the decision making. • To explain how individuals make rational decisions using marginal analysis. • To understand how incentives influence decision making. • To explore how trade, markets, and government shape resource allocation. • To apply principles to analyze everyday choices and economic policies. ECONOMICS AND IT’S IMPORTANCE • The word economy is derived from the Greek word oikonomos- meaning “one who manage a household.” • Like Household faces many decision making, a society faces as well The major questions regarding economic decision making are ✓Who will work? ✓What goods should be produced? ✓What resources should be used in production? ✓At what price of the goods and services should be sold in the market? WHAT IS ECONOMICS Society and Scarce Resources: ➢The management of society’s resources is important because resources are scarce. ➢Scarcity. . . means that society

section_label: CHAPTER TITLE: TEN PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS
text: has limited resources and therefore cannot produce all the goods and services people wish to have. WHAT IS ECONOMICS Scarcity vs Shortage Scarcity: • Permanent condition • Exists everywhere • Due to limited resources vs unlimited wants Shortage: • Temporary condition • Market-specific • Due to price or supply disruptions WHAT IS ECONOMICS ➢Economics is the science of scarcity. ➢Scarcity is a situation where our wants are more than our resources. ➢Since we are unable to have everything we desire, we must make choices. ➢Economics is the study of Choices. ➢In economics we will study the choices of individuals, firms, and governments. ➢In Economics we study how society manages its scarce resources. ➢Economics, as a social science is concerned with the optimum utilization of limited resources for achieving satisfaction of economic wants. MICROECONOMICS & MACROECONOMICS ➢Microeconomics focuses on the individual units of the economy. ▪How households and firms make decisions and how they interact in specific markets ➢Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole. ▪Economy-wide phenomena, including inflation, unemployment, and economic growth ➢These two branches of economics are closely

section_label: CHAPTER TITLE: TEN PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS
text: intertwined, yet distinct – they address different questions. MICROECONOMICS ➢Study of the economic actions of individuals and small groups of individuals ➢The study of particular firm, particular household; individual prices, wages, and incomes; individual industry; particular commodities. ➢ Microeconomics proceeds to examine how resources are allocated by households, individual industries and individual firms operating under industry and how the prices of various products of these individual firms are established . MACROECONOMICS ➢Macroeconomics deals with how the economy functions as a whole, including how the economy’s total output of goods and services, the price level of goods and services and the total employment of resources are determined and what causes fluctuations in these economic variables. ➢ Macroeconomics studies the relationship and interaction between the factors and forces that determine the level and growth of output and employment, general price level of an economy. PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMICS ➢How people make decisions
People face tradeoffs.
The cost of something is what you give up to get it.
Rational people think at the margin.
People respond to incentives. ➢How People Interact
Trade can make everyone better off.
Markets are usually a good way to organize economic activity.
Governments can sometimes improve market outcomes. ➢How the economy as a whole works
The standard of living depends on a country’s ability to produce goods and services.
Prices rise when the government prints too much money.

text: Principle 1: People Face Tradeoffs “There is no such thing as a free lunch” This means that there are always trade-offs - to get more of something we like, we have to give up something else that we like. For example, if you spend money on mobile phone and you won't be able to spend it on new laptop. To get one thing, we usually have to give up another thing since the resources we have to satisfy wants are scarce. Trade-offs are all the alternatives that we must give up to get one good instead of another. ✓Guns vs. butter ✓Savings vs. clothing or family vacation ✓Study time vs. Party time ✓Efficiency vs. equality Principle 1: People Face Tradeoffs Efficiency vs. Equality ✓Efficiency means society gets the most that it can from its scarce resources. ✓Equality means the benefits of those resources are distributed fairly among the members of society. Tradeoff: ✓In order to achieve equality, Government could redistribute money from rich to poor. ✓But this step reduces incentive to work and produce more which affects the economic growth.

text: Principle 2: The Cost of Something is What You Give Up to Get it Decisions require comparing costs and benefits of alternatives. ✓Whether to go to college or to work? ✓Whether to study or go out on a visit to a place? ✓Whether to go to class or sleep in? The opportunity cost of an item is what you give up to obtain that item. Going to college for a year is not just the tuition fees, books, and other fees, but also the foregone wages. Seeing a movie is not just the price of the ticket, but the value of the time you spend in the theater. Principle 2: The Cost of Something is What You Give Up to Get it The opportunity cost of an item is the cost of next best alternative sacrificed or forgone. A machine can produce either X or Y. The opportunity cost of producing a given quantity of X is, therefore, the quantity of Y which it would have produced. If that machine can produce 10

Principle 3: Rational People Think at the Margin. Example ➢Alex is preparing for his math exam and is thinking about whether to study an extra hour. If he studies for one more hour, he expects to gain 5 additional exam points. Since each exam point is worth about $2 to him, the marginal benefit of that hour is $10. But studying means he has to give up an $8 wage from his coffee shop job, which is the marginal cost. Because the marginal benefit ($10) is greater than the marginal cost ($8), it makes sense for Alex to study the extra hour. ➢However, if Alex decides to study a second additional hour, the benefits start to decline: this time, he can only earn 3 extra exam points, which equals $6 in value. Now the marginal benefit ($6) is less than the marginal cost ($8). Since the cost outweighs the benefit, Alex should stop after the first hour. Principle 5: Trade Can Make Everyone Better Off ➢People gain from their ability to trade with one another. ➢People can specialize in producing one good or service in which they are efficient and exchange it for other goods with other persons. ➢Countries also benefit from trade due to their ability to specialize in producing goods and services. ✓Competition results in gains from trading ✓Get a better price abroad for goods they produce ✓Buy other goods more cheaply from abroad than could be produced at home Principle 6: Markets Are Usually a Good Way to Organize

text: Economic Activity. ➢A market economy is an economy that allocates resources through the decentralized decisions of many firms and households as they interact in markets for goods and services. ✓Households decide what to buy and who to work for. ✓Firms decide whom to hire and what to produce. ✓Adam Smith made the observation that households and firms interacting in markets act as if guided by an “invisible hand.” ✓Because households and firms look at prices when deciding what to buy and sell, they unknowingly take into account the social costs of their actions. ✓As a result, prices guide decision makers to reach outcomes that tend to maximize the welfare of society as a whole. Principle 7: Governments Can Sometimes Improve Market Outcomes. ➢We need government ✓Enforce the rules ✓Enforce property rights (Ability of an individual to own and exercise control over scarce resources) ➢Market failure occurs when the market fails to allocate resources efficiently. ➢Market failure may be caused by ✓an externality, which is the impact of one person or firm’s actions on the well-being of a bystander. ✓market power,

Principle 7: Governments Can Sometimes Improve Market Outcomes. ➢When the market fails (breaks down) government can intervene to promote efficiency and equality. ✓To promote efficiency : Avoid market failure ✓To promote equality : Avoid disparities in economic wellbeing ✓If the market’s distribution of economic well-being is not desirable, tax or welfare policies can change how the economic “pie” is divided. text: • When individuals make decisions, they face tradeoffs among alternative goals. • The cost of any action is measured in terms of foregone opportunities. • Rational people make decisions by comparing marginal costs and marginal benefits. • People change their behavior in response to the incentives they face.

• Trade can be mutually beneficial. • Markets are usually a good way of coordinating trade among people. • Government can potentially improve market outcomes if there is some market failure or if the market outcome is inequitable.
